horizon_driver: upstream project cycle (FID to first oil/gas is 3-7 years) and multi-decade reserve life; NOCs additionally run on dynastic/regime horizons (15-25 years), while listed majors face nearer-term shareholder pressure that periodically overrides the long asset horizon

capabilities.note: maintain current capex guidance and production plan
restore/expand low-carbon capex line, accept host-state or regulatory transition demands
take a major upstream FID or lock in a long-term LNG offtake contract — multi-decade capital commitment, very costly to unwind once sanctioned

constraints.source: BP scrapped its 2030 production-cut target entirely in 2025 (CEO: company had gone 'too far, too fast'), cutting renewables capex from ~$5bn/yr to $1-2bn/yr while raising oil & gas capex to $10bn/yr; Shell dropped its 2035 emissions-reduction pledge in March 2026 and is targeting +1m boe/d oil and gas growth by 2030 in tension with its own 2050 net-zero goal — https://www.tipranks.com/news/bp-vows-to-drill-baby-drill-as-oil-major-slashes-renewables-to-boost-fossil-fuel-output ; https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/021026-shell-casts-doubt-on-net-zero-2050-commitment
constraints.breaks_under: shareholder pressure for near-term returns, activist investor campaigns, or a sustained high-price environment rewarding volume growth

constraints.source: Saudi Aramco's variable dividend collapsed from ~$43bn (2024) to ~$880m (2025) while the base dividend ($84.6bn) was held and partly debt-funded to support the Saudi state budget; government debt is projected to rise to 32.7% of GDP in 2026 — https://www.energyconnects.com/news/oil/2025/march/aramco-cuts-world-s-biggest-dividend-in-blow-to-saudi-budget/ ; https://agsi.org/analysis/putting-the-2026-saudi-budget-under-the-microscope/
constraints.breaks_under: for NOCs, sponsoring-state fiscal need dominates minority-shareholder return expectations whenever oil price falls below the state's effective breakeven (~$72-85/bbl range cited for Saudi 2026 budget)

stated_vs_revealed.stated: Shell and BP formally adopted net-zero-by-2050 targets (c. 2020-2021) with interim production-reduction and renewables-investment milestones, marketed as a managed energy transition.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: BP scrapped its 2030 oil-and-gas production-cut target in 2025 and is now growing production toward 2.3-2.5m bbl/d (implying ~9% growth vs a prior planned 25% cut), cutting renewables spend to $1-2bn/yr and raising oil & gas capex to $10bn/yr. Shell dropped its 2035 emissions pledge in March 2026 and is targeting oil & gas growth that its own reporting flags as in tension with its 2050 goal.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: The transition pledges were priced options exercised only while capital markets rewarded ESG positioning; once shareholder pressure and a softer 2025-26 renewables return profile shifted, both majors reverted to hydrocarbon-volume growth as the revealed preference.

stated_vs_revealed.stated: Saudi Aramco presents itself as a shareholder-value-maximizing IOC-style company with a progressive dividend policy.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: The variable (performance-linked) dividend was gutted (-98%, $43bn to $880m) between 2024 and 2025 while the $84.6bn base dividend was preserved via increased leverage, precisely because that base dividend is the primary funding line for the Saudi state budget — upstream capex guidance ($52-58bn for 2025) was maintained even as payouts to minority shareholders were cut.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: Aramco is a fiscal instrument of the Saudi state first and a shareholder-return vehicle second; capex commitments to sustain long-run production capacity are more durable than any specific payout promise.

dependencies.type: sponsoring state for Aramco/ADNOC — capex and dividend policy set to serve state fiscal needs
physical routing, blending and sanctions-arbitrage of crude/product flows
insurability of tanker routes and terminals in conflict zones
sanctions regimes and export-control policy affecting which crude grades and buyers are reachable

tripwires.if: Brent trades above ~$90/bbl for two or more consecutive quarters
tripwires.then: upstream capex guidance is raised across multiple majors within 1-2 quarters — the revealed preference is volume growth over price restraint, not the reverse
tripwires.source: pattern consistent with Aramco/ADNOC/Exxon capex guidance behaviour cited above

tripwires.then: NOCs preserve upstream capex and raise sovereign/corporate debt before cutting production or capex — payouts to minority shareholders (variable dividends) are cut first, as the Aramco 2024-25 sequence shows

tripwires.if: a major publicly reaffirms a net-zero or production-cut pledge under investor/activist pressure
tripwires.then: treat it as cheap talk with a 2-4 year reversal risk once oil prices firm or shareholder composition shifts — both BP and Shell reversed comparable pledges within roughly 3-5 years of adoption

what_would_change_my_mind: A major sustaining a renewables-capex increase and a production-cut trajectory through a period of both high oil prices AND shareholder pressure to grow hydrocarbon output would falsify the 'transition pledges are performative' finding. Also watch Aramco's 2026 full-year capex figure (not yet reported as of this writing) — a cut below the $52-58bn guided range would indicate the state-fiscal-support constraint has started to bind on upstream investment itself, not just on dividends.
